title: Your AI games look generic because of one mistake
author: Diligent-Hat-6509
selftext:
If you ask AI for a genre, you get the average of that genre. That's why so many AI games look the same.

For my last game I started with one sentence, a feeling instead of a genre: "a cabin, hot tea, and a blizzard outside the window." AI built everything (ChatGPT for references, Claude in Blender, Codex in Unreal), and I only made the decisions, in 4 steps:

1. \*\*Goal:\*\* one sentence. A feeling, not a genre.

2. \*\*Reference:\*\* make the feeling visible. Skip images that are pretty but not yours, and keep the happy accidents. ChatGPT randomly added a tiny red figure, and he became my main character.

3. \*\*Rules:\*\* turn the feeling into rules AI can follow, like "soft, never sharp" or "only shelter is warm".

4. \*\*Check:\*\* every decision has to pass one question: "does this feel like sitting in a cabin with tea, watching the storm?"

When the first trees came out too sharp, I didn't have to explain anything. My rule says soft, so everything got rounder.



What's your trick for avoiding the generic AI look?

comments.body: Good point. If we start off by putting it in a pigeonhole it'll stay there.

comments.author: HattyH99
comments.body: Nice, def a big issue with anything AI related, bad prompts lead to generic texts, 2d art and games. Most of the time AI generates very generic results since it's basing it off the most common and most used format.

replies.author: Diligent-Hat-6509
replies.body: Exactly, hopefuly this video helps people who don't know how to make better prompts.

comments.author: FDAlchemistDev
comments.body:
This is something screenwriters, and writers in general, use in front of a blank page: start from a feeling, not a genre. A genre gives you the average, a feeling gives you inspiration.

I think your video can inspire people to use AI models to create, not just to replicate.
If they apply what you're showing, they can find new ways to express themselves. That's the real opportunity we get with AI breaking into game development.

And your "check" step is the one most people skip: a rule only matters once something fails it, like your sharp trees.

Starting from a feeling is one of the reasons I came to gamedev, and why I love vibecoding.

...and the freedom to see your projects come alive without gatekeepers.

...and a bigger audience that's (hopefully) more interested in playing than in reading.

replies.author: Diligent-Hat-6509
replies.body:
Thanks, this is exactly what I was trying to get across with the video. I really like the way you put it too: “a genre gives you the average, a feeling gives you inspiration.” That pretty much sums up the whole idea better than I did 😄

And yeah, the CHECK part became way more important than I expected. A lot of the actual art direction came from seeing something that technically fit the prompt, but just *felt wrong*, and then figuring out why.

replies.author: FDAlchemistDev
replies.body:
Trust me, your video is a great resource like it's your post.
And yeah, understand what we feel is wrong in something that looks good is that attention of detail that you get with experience. Very, very hard!

replies.author: sw3d
replies.body: If you don't mind me asking, what is your setup for content creation - are you editing / producing the clips with AI?

replies.author: Diligent-Hat-6509
replies.body:
Sure, I do most of the creative work myself. I prepare and record all the footage, write the script, and plan out the scenes in text. Then I use AI to check the script, mainly to make sure the English sounds natural and to suggest better wording when something feels off.

For editing, I use DaVinci Resolve and put the scenes together myself. I also use Claude for some of the more technical stuff, like motion graphics or visualizing ideas that I know I want but don’t necessarily know how to create from scratch. I also use Claude for cinematic shots. I set up what I want and it handles recording those shots directly in Unreal Engine.

So AI is definitely a big part of the workflow, but mostly as a tool that helps me execute the ideas and direction I already have in mind.
